theorem.content:
\label{thm:main-theorem-intro}
  Let $p>3$ be prime. Let $K$ be a $p$-adic field that is totally ramified over $\Q_p$. Let $E_1$ and $E_2$ be elliptic curves defined over $K$ with full $K$-rational 2-torsion and supersingular reduction. Then for any $n>0$, there exists a WR relation $\{P_1,P_2\}_{K/K}=0$ in $K(K;E_1,E_2)$ of signature $(n,n)$.
theorem.label: thm:main-theorem-intro

post_theorem_intro_text:
The WR relations produced in Theorem \ref{thm:main-theorem-intro} come from genus 2 covers of $E_1$ and $E_2$. More precisely, there is a WR relation in $K(K;E_1,E_2)$ for every curve $C$ over $K$, whose Jacobian can be mapped into $E_1\times E_2$, and a choice of rational function $f\in K(C)^\times$. In this paper, we use a construction due to J. Scholten of a genus 2 curve $C$ and explicit nonconstant maps $\f_1:C\rightarrow E_1$ and $\f_2:C\rightarrow E_2$. Since $C$ is hyperelliptic it has particularly simple principal divisors, so the choice of rational function can be made flexibly. Armed with a suitable choice of $C,\f_1,\f_2$ and $f$, we can then $p$-adically approximate the resulting WR relation to determine its signature.

This paper is organized into three sections. In section \ref{sec:prelim}, we review all the basic theory we will need about formal groups of elliptic curves, supersingular reduction, and the Somekawa $K$-group for products of elliptic curves. Along the way we define the signature of a $K/K$-symbol and determine the type and quantity of WR relations one needs to show the vanishing of all $K/K$-symbols modulo $p$. In section \ref{sec:scholten_curves} we review the construction of the hyperelliptic curves that map to $E_1\times E_2$, compute the WR relations they produce, and use them to prove Theorem \ref{thm:main-theorem-intro}. Lastly, in section \ref{sec:computations}, we focus on the case of quadratic ramified extensions $K$ and present computational evidence that the genus 2 spans of section \ref{sec:scholten_curves} produce the necessary WR relations to show that all $K/K$-symbols vanish modulo $p$.

The paper uses a construction of J.~Scholten to build a genus 2 hyperelliptic curve $C$ and explicit nonconstant maps $\f_1:C\to E_1$ and $\f_2:C\to E_2$; since $C$ is hyperelliptic and has "particularly simple principal divisors," the rational function $f$ can be chosen flexibly. With a suitable choice of $C,\f_1,\f_2,$ and $f$, one then "$p$-adically approximate[s] the resulting WR relation to determine its signature" (producing signature $(n,n)$).

mcq.question: Let $p>3$ be a prime, let $K$ be a $p$-adic field totally ramified over $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and let $E_1,E_2$ be elliptic curves over $K$ with full $K$-rational $2$-torsion and supersingular reduction. Under these assumptions, which statement is universally true for all such $(p,K,E_1,E_2)$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For every integer $n>0$, there exists a WR relation $\{P_1,P_2\}_{K/K}=0$ in the Somekawa $K$-group $K(K;E_1,E_2)$ whose signature is $(n,n)$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For every integer $n>0$, there exists a WR relation $\{P_1,P_2\}_{K/K}=0$ in $K(K;E_1,E_2)$ whose signature is $(n,n)$, and moreover the same relation can be chosen to arise from a genus $2$ hyperelliptic curve $C/K$ with maps $\varphi_i:C\to E_i$ such that the auxiliary function $f\in K(C)^\times$ may be taken to be defined over $K$ with divisor supported entirely on $K$-rational points of $C$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists at least one nontrivial WR relation $\{P_1,P_2\}_{K/K}=0$ in the Somekawa $K$-group $K(K;E_1,E_2)$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists an integer $n_0>0$ (depending only on $p$ and $K$) such that for every pair $(E_1,E_2)$ as above and every $n\ge n_0$, there exists a WR relation $\{P_1,P_2\}_{K/K}=0$ in $K(K;E_1,E_2)$ of signature $(n,n)$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For every integer $n>0$, there exists a WR relation $\{P_1,P_2\}_{K/K}=0$ in $K(K;E_1,E_2)$ of signature $(n,n)$ that can be chosen so that it is induced by a genus $2$ cover $C\to E_1$ and $C\to E_2$ with $C/K$ hyperelliptic and having good reduction over $\mathcal{O}_K$.

TAS.justification: The question is not a definitional restatement; it asks for a universally valid conclusion under a fairly specific arithmetic-geometric setup, with options varying in strength (existence vs. uniformity vs. geometric realizability).

GPS.justification: Selecting the universally true statement requires understanding subtle distinctions: existence of WR relations vs. existence for every signature (n,n), and whether additional geometric constraints (good reduction, rational divisor support, uniform n0) are guaranteed. This demands genuine comparative reasoning about what the hypotheses do and do not force.

They are distinct and aligned with realistic misconceptions about effectivity/uniformity and geometric realizations.

\begin{theorem}\label{theo:e-final}
	Let $G\in \{SO(N),U(N), SU(N)\}$. Fix an edge $e$ and let $s$ be a collection of strings.  The following identity holds 
	\begin{equs}[e15]
		{}&\Big(-2 \,r(s)\,c_\mfg+2\nu \big(r(s)-t(e)^2\big)\Big) \phi(s)
		\\	=
		&\mp\beta \sum_{s' \in \mD^\pm_e(s) } \phi(s')
		\mp\kappa \sum_{s' \in \mB^\pm_e(s) } \phi(s')\mp 2\mu \sum_{s' \in \mT^\pm_e(s) } \phi(s')
		\mp 2\lambda\sum_{s' \in \mS^\pm_e(s) } \phi(s')
		\\
		&\mp 2\lambda \sum_{s' \in \mM^\pm_{e,U}(s) } \phi(s')
		\mp 2\mu \sum_{s' \in \mM^\pm_{e,\backslash U}(s) } \phi(s')\mp 2\lambda \sum_{s' \in \mX^\pm_{e,U}(s) } \phi(s')
		\mp 2\mu \sum_{s' \in \mX^\pm_{e,\backslash U}(s) } \phi(s') \\
		&\mp	\beta\nu \sum_{s' \in \mE^\pm_{e,\square}(s) } \phi(s')
		\mp\kappa\nu \sum_{s' \in \mE^\pm_{e,\parallel}(s) } \phi(s').
	\end{equs}
	Here $c_\mfg$ is as in \eqref{e:c_g} and 
	$\lambda,\mu, \nu$ in as in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-nu}.
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
After all the operations are precisely defined, we will state the above theorem
more explicitly, see Theorem~\ref{theo:e-final} and Theorem~\ref{theo:x-final}.

\begin{remark}\label{rem:no-N}
In this article  $N$ is fixed. One could also consider large $N$ problems using the 
Makeenko--Migdal equations. In this case, typically $\beta,\kappa$
in \eqref{e:CS}
will depend on $N$.  
For instance the Yang--Mills term will be replaced by 
$N\beta  \Re \sum_{p} \mathrm{Tr}(Q_p)$,
which is the well-known t'Hooft scaling for the coupling $\beta$. 
In such settings, our Theorem~\ref{theo:main} then still holds with a simple change of variables $\beta,\kappa$. 
\end{remark}

Our main tool to prove Theorem~\ref{theo:main} is 
the Langevin dynamics, or stochastic quantization, 
as well as It\^o's formula. 
The dynamical approach was used to derive the Makeenko--Migdal equations
for the pure lattice Yang--Mills model without a Higgs field
\cite{SSZloop} (originally proved by \cite{Cha,Jafar}, see also \cite{CPS2023}).
Following the approach therein, we would consider 
the Langevin dynamics of  the measure \eqref{e:LYMH}
\begin{equ}[e:LSDE]
	\dif (Q,\Phi) = \nabla \mathcal S_\YMH (Q,\Phi) \dif t + \sqrt 2\dif \mathfrak B\;,
\end{equ}
where $\nabla$ is the gradient and $\mathfrak B$ is  the  Brownian motion on 
the product Riemannian manifold $\cQ_L=G^{E^+_\Lambda}\times M^\Lambda$. 
We refer to \cite[Section~2.1]{SZZ22} or \cite{SZZYMH} for detailed review 
on the geometry background.
In this paper we actually consider an improved approach, by studying the  
 Langevin dynamics of the {\it conditional} measure,
fixing all the variables except at one single edge $e$ or lattice site $x$.
Namely, a dynamic given by an stochastic differential equation (SDE for short) on $G$ or $M$, see \eqref{eq:YM1}.
We will give more explicit forms for this equation in Section~\ref{sec:YMHSDEs}.

In Section~\ref{sec:strings}, we precisely define 
the operations on strings. In Section~\ref{sec:Ito}, we prove our main
theorem.  There are multiple motivations to derive the 
 Makeenko--Migdal equations for the YMH model.
For lattice pure Yang--Mills,
such equations \cite{Cha,Jafar,SSZloop,OmarRon,CPS2023}
have been used to study (or have close connection with)
gauge-string duality, surface summations, large $N$ properties, area law,
and properties of the model in 2D, see  
\cite{Cha,ChatterjeeJafar,MR3861073,CPS2023,Cao2025area,borga2024surface}.
Hopefully our Makeenko--Migdal equations in Theorem~\ref{theo:main}
will also be useful to study these questions for the YMH model,
for example the question of surface sums where the surfaces have boundaries which arise from the Wilson line observables, or whether there are  transitions between area law and perimeter law depending on the parameters $N,d,\beta,\kappa$. 

Moreover, in the continuum 2D case,  the Makeenko--Migdal equations
for pure Yang--Mills \cite{Levy11,MR3554890,Driver17,MR3982691,PPSY2023}
play a significant role in the study of the model, and they can be derived as 
the continuum limit of the lattice Makeenko--Migdal equations, see \cite{SSZ2d}.
However, in continuum, these equations are not known once another field such as Higgs is coupled in the model, even in 2D. It would be interesting to see if our Theorem~\ref{theo:main} would give some hint on the formulation of such equations
for 2D YMH (note that the scaling limit approach in  \cite{SSZ2d} does not directly apply to YMH here since it relies on the special structures of 2D pure YM).
We leave these questions to future studies.

theorem.content:
\label{main-intro}
Let $\mu, \tau > 1/2$. Set $\alpha_\mu = (j^{1/\mu})_{j \in \N}$ and  $\alpha_\tau = (j^{1/\tau})_{j \in \N}$. Then,
$$
\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)} \cong \Lambda(\alpha_\mu, \alpha_\tau).
$$
theorem.label: main-intro

post_theorem_intro_text:
The proof of Theorem \ref{main-intro} combines the Pe\l czy\'nski-Vogt decomposition result for the $(\PLS)$-type power series spaces $\Lambda_{\infty}(\alpha,\beta)$ of infinite type with properties of Gabor frames---a fundamental tool in time-frequency analysis \cite{G-FoundTFAnalysis}. In \cite{D-N-SeqSpRepBBSp}, we used the same technique to obtain sequence space representations for Gelfand-Shilov spaces, in particular $\Sigma^{\mu}_{\tau}$. The restriction $\mu, \tau > 1/2$ is imposed because we rely on a result on dual windows of Gabor frames from \cite{Janssen}. 
Finally, we note that in  \cite{D-N-WeighPLBUltradiffFuncMultSp, D-N-BarrelWeighPLBUltradiffFunc} we also made use of time-frequency analysis, namely, the short-time Fourier transform \cite{G-FoundTFAnalysis}, which can be seen as a continuous version of Gabor frames.

\subsection{Outline of the paper} Section \ref{sect-prelim} collects notation and preliminary notions. In Section \ref{sect-seqsp}, we define and discuss various sequence spaces. We prove a splitting result for $(\PLS)$-type sequence spaces in Section \ref{sect-splitting}. This section is based on \cite{K-SplitPowerSeriesSpPLS}. Section \ref{sect-PV} is devoted to the proof of the  Pe\l czy\'nski-Vogt decomposition result for $(\PLS)$-type power series spaces. In Section \ref{sect-appl}, we apply this result to obtain sequence space representations for multiplier spaces of Gelfand-Shilov spaces of Beurling type. In particular, we show Theorem \ref{main-intro} there.

The proof of Theorem \ref{main-intro} \emph{combines} the Pe\l czy\'nski-Vogt decomposition result for the $(\PLS)$-type power series spaces $\Lambda_{\infty}(\alpha,\beta)$ of infinite type with properties of Gabor frames. The restriction $\mu,\tau>1/2$ is imposed because the argument relies on a result on dual windows of Gabor frames.

According to the paper outline, the route to Theorem~\ref{main-intro} is: develop notation and preliminaries (Section~\ref{sect-prelim}); define and discuss sequence spaces (Section~\ref{sect-seqsp}); prove a splitting result for $(\PLS)$-type sequence spaces (Section~\ref{sect-splitting}); prove the Pe\l czy\'nski-Vogt decomposition result for $(\PLS)$-type power series spaces (Section~\ref{sect-PV}); then apply this to obtain sequence space representations for multiplier spaces of Gelfand-Shilov spaces of Beurling type (Section~\ref{sect-appl}), where Theorem~\ref{main-intro} is shown.

mcq.question: Let \(\mu,\tau>\tfrac12\). Define the sequences \(\alpha_\mu=(j^{1/\mu})_{j\in\mathbb N}\) and \(\alpha_\tau=(j^{1/\tau})_{j\in\mathbb N}\). Under these assumptions, which statement holds for every such pair \((\mu,\tau)\)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: The space \(\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)}\) is isomorphic to \(\Lambda(\alpha_\mu,\alpha_\tau)\), i.e. \(\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)}\cong\Lambda(\alpha_\mu,\alpha_\tau)\).

choices.label: B
choices.text:
Let \(\mu,\tau>\tfrac12\). With \(\alpha_\mu=(j^{1/\mu})_{j\in\mathbb N}\) and \(\alpha_\tau=(j^{1/\tau})_{j\in\mathbb N}\), one has the canonical topological isomorphism
\[
\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)}\cong \Lambda_{\infty}(\alpha_\mu,\alpha_\tau).
\]

choices.label: C
choices.text: Let \(\mu,\tau>\tfrac12\). With \(\alpha_\mu=(j^{1/\mu})_{j\in\mathbb N}\) and \(\alpha_\tau=(j^{1/\tau})_{j\in\mathbb N}\), the space \(\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)}\) admits a continuous linear embedding as a complemented subspace of \(\Lambda(\alpha_\mu,\alpha_\tau)\).

choices.label: D
choices.text:
For every \(\mu,\tau>\tfrac12\), with \(\alpha_\mu=(j^{1/\mu})_{j\in\mathbb N}\) and \(\alpha_\tau=(j^{1/\tau})_{j\in\mathbb N}\), there exists \(C=C(\mu,\tau)>0\) such that
\[
\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)}\cong \Lambda(C\alpha_\mu,\alpha_\tau)
\]
(as locally convex spaces).

choices.label: E
choices.text:
Let \(\mu,\tau\ge \tfrac12\). Define \(\alpha_\mu=(j^{1/\mu})_{j\in\mathbb N}\) and \(\alpha_\tau=(j^{1/\tau})_{j\in\mathbb N}\). Then
\[
\mathcal{Z}^{(\mu)}_{(\tau)}\cong \Lambda(\alpha_\mu,\alpha_\tau).
\]

sketch:
To prove Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, the paper first reduces to triangulations: it is stated that “every 3-colored planar graph is the induced subgraph of some 3-colored triangulation,” by “adding a new vertex in a non-triangular face,” and since “a 3-slopes segment representation of a triangulation naturally induces such a representation for its induced subgraphs,” it “restrict[s] ourselves to the case of triangulations.”

Then the proof proceeds via “triangular contact schemes,” described as “particular 3-slopes contact segment representations of an auxiliary graph,” with the key intermediate claim that “every 3-colorable triangulation admits such a scheme.” Finally, “those schemes are used … to build 3-slopes segment representations.”

mcq.question: Let $G$ be any planar graph whose vertices are partitioned into three color classes (i.e., $G$ is given with a 3-coloring). Which statement is universally true for every such 3-colored planar graph?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists a segment representation of $G$ in the plane using only three slopes, such that vertices in the same color class are represented by parallel segments (equivalently, each color class corresponds to one of the three segment directions).

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists a segment representation of $G$ in the plane using only three slopes, such that vertices in the same color class are represented by parallel segments, and moreover the three slopes can be fixed in advance (e.g., $0,\pi/3,2\pi/3$) independently of $G$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists a segment representation of $G$ in the plane in which vertices in the same color class are represented by parallel segments (with no restriction on the number of slopes used).

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists a 3-slopes segment representation of $G$ in the plane such that two vertices are adjacent in $G$ if and only if their corresponding segments intersect, and parallel segments correspond to the color classes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: There exists a 3-slopes segment representation of $G$ in the plane such that parallel segments correspond to the color classes and, in addition, the representation can be chosen as a contact representation (segments are interior-disjoint and adjacencies correspond exactly to segment endpoints touching).

TAS.justification: If the intended target is the known result about 3-slope segment representations respecting a given 3-coloring, then choice A is essentially that theorem stated in answer form. The question is still nontrivial because it asks to select the correct universal statement among close variants, but it is largely a recognition/recollection check rather than an application.

They are distinct and aligned with realistic failure modes.

theorem.label: lem:minimaxless

sketch:
For any $\x_0\in X$ we have
\[\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in Y} f(\x_0,\mathbf{y}) \leq \inf_{\mathbf{y}\in Y} \sup_{\mathbf{x}\in X} f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).\]
Taking the supremum over $\x_0\in X$ gives \eqref{eq:minimaxless}.
expanded_sketch:
For any $\x_0\in X$ we have
\[\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in Y} f(\x_0,\mathbf{y}) \leq \inf_{\mathbf{y}\in Y} \sup_{\mathbf{x}\in X} f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).\]
Taking the supremum over $\x_0\in X$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:minimaxless}
\sup_{\x\in X} \inf_{\y\in Y} f(\x,\y) \leq \inf_{\y\in Y} \sup_{\x\in X} f(\x,\y).
\end{equation}
.

theorem.content:
\label{thm: bounded Fatou components are Jordan domains}
    Let $f(z)=ae^z+be^{-z}$ be a cosine function. Suppose that $P(f)$ is bounded, $U$ is a bounded Fatou component, which is not eventually mapped to a Siegel disk. Then $U$ is a Jordan domain.
theorem.label: thm: bounded Fatou components are Jordan domains

sketch: The post-theorem introduction indicates that Theorem~\ref{thm: bounded Fatou components are Jordan domains} is proved “using the puzzle”: specifically, “Section~\ref{sec: construction of puzzles} constructed the Yoccoz puzzle for cosine functions with bounded post-critical set,” and “Section~\ref{sec: local connectivity of bounded Fatou components} proved Theorem~\ref{thm: bounded Fatou components are Jordan domains} using the puzzle.”
expanded_theorem:
\label{thm: bounded Fatou components are Jordan domains}
    Let $f(z)=ae^z+be^{-z}$ be a cosine function. Suppose that $P(f)$ is bounded, $U$ is a bounded Fatou component, which is not eventually mapped to a Siegel disk. Then $U$ is a Jordan domain.,

mcq.question: Let $f(z)=ae^z+be^{-z}$ be a cosine function such that its postsingular set $P(f)$ is bounded. Let $U$ be a bounded Fatou component of $f$ with the property that there is no $n\ge 0$ for which $f^{\circ n}(U)$ is a Siegel disk. Under these assumptions, which statement is universally true for every such Fatou component $U$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: $U$ is a Jordan domain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: $U$ is a Jordan domain, and moreover $\partial U$ is a $C^{1+\alpha}$-smooth curve for some $\alpha>0$ (depending only on $f$).

choices.label: C
choices.text: $U$ is simply connected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If $U$ is a bounded Fatou component that is not eventually mapped to a Siegel disk, then for every $n\ge 0$ the iterate $f^{\circ n}(U)$ is a Jordan domain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Let $f(z)=ae^z+be^{-z}$ be a cosine function and let $U$ be a bounded Fatou component not eventually mapped to a Siegel disk. Then $U$ is a Jordan domain (no boundedness assumption on $P(f)$ is needed).

sketch_usage_meta.label: B
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: upgraded boundary regularity from Jordan to $C^{1+\alpha}$

sketch_usage_meta.label: C
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: dropped boundary-local-connectivity/Jordan conclusion, kept only simple connectivity

sketch_usage_meta.label: D
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: strengthened conclusion from $U$ to all forward images $f^{\circ n}(U)$ being Jordan

sketch_usage_meta.label: E
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: removed boundedness of postsingular set $P(f)$ hypothesis needed for the Yoccoz puzzle setup

ALS.justification: The stem does not give away the conclusion (Jordan domain) and does not contain phrasing that points uniquely to choice A. It states hypotheses and asks for a universal conclusion.

TAS.justification: The question is not a direct restatement of a named theorem in the stem; it requires selecting the correct strength of conclusion among several nearby alternatives (Jordan vs smoother boundary, vs simply connected, vs forward images, vs dropping hypotheses).

GPS.justification: To answer, a solver must reason about what boundedness of the postsingular set buys (e.g., puzzle/LC boundary technology), what exclusions (no eventual Siegel) eliminate, and which conclusions are known to be true vs common overstrengthenings. The correct option is not obvious without substantive domain knowledge.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target typical failure modes: (B) over-regularity upgrade, (C) weaker true statement, (D) overgeneralizing to all iterates, (E) dropping a key hypothesis. They are distinct and closely aligned with realistic mathematical confusions.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: High-quality MCQ: no answer leakage, non-tautological, requires genuine theorem-level reasoning about complex dynamics hypotheses, and includes strong, well-targeted distractors that reflect common overstrengthening/weakening errors.

theorem.content:
\label{My work}
    Conjecture \ref{Generalized Franchetta Conjecture} is true for genus $g=11$.
theorem.label: My work

post_theorem_intro_text:
Our method is based on exploiting Mukai's program for genus $11$ curves and K3 surfaces, which provides a birational bridge between the moduli space of K3 surfaces and the moduli space of curves. The main result of Mukai's program in genus $11$ is stated as follows:
\begin{theorem}[Mukai's program in genus $11$ \cite{Muk}]
\label{Mukai's program}
    Let $\mathcal P$ be the $\mathbb{P}^{11}$-bundle over $\cF_{11}'$ parametrizing 
$$\{[S,\mathcal{L},C]\mid(S,\mathcal{L})\in 
\mathcal{F}_{11}',C \in |\mathcal{L}|\}.$$
Then the rational map $\phi:\mathcal P\dashrightarrow \cM_{11}$ mapping $[S,\mathcal L,C]$ to the curve $C$ is a birational map. Here, $\cM_{11}$ is the moduli stack of smooth curves of genus $11$.
\end{theorem}
\indent This birational equivalence allows us to transfer the problem to a problem about the moduli space of curves. Specifically, we show that the Chow group $\operatorname {CH}^2(\cS_{11}')_\mathbb{Q}$ can be controlled by the Chow group $\operatorname {CH}^2(\cF_{11}')_\mathbb{Q}$ and the Chow group $\operatorname {CH}^2(\overline{M}_{11,1})_\mathbb{Q}$ of the coarse moduli space $\overline{M}_{11,1}$ of stable genus $11$ curves with one marked point.\\
\indent Another key ingredient is the following result on the tautological generation of the second Chow group of the coarse moduli space of pointed curves.
\begin{theorem}
\label{CH2 is tautologically generated for rationally connected moduli space introduction}
    Suppose $2g-2+n>0$, and the coarse moduli space $\overline{M}_{g,n}$ is rationally connected. Then $\operatorname {CH}^2(\overline{M}_{g,n})_\mathbb{Q}$ is generated by tautological classes.
\end{theorem}
By \cite[Corollary 2]{Bar}, the coarse moduli space $\overline{M}_{11,1}$ is rationally connected. Therefore,~$\operatorname {CH}^2(\overline{M}_{11,1})_\mathbb{Q}$ is tautologically generated. This complete description of $\operatorname {CH}^2(\overline{M}_{11,1})_\mathbb{Q}$, combined with the bridge provided by Mukai's program, allows us to conclude the proof of Theorem \ref{My work}.\\
\indent This article is organized as follows. In Section \ref{Section: Reduction to moduli of curve}, we exploit Mukai's program to relate the generalized Franchetta conjecture in genus $11$ to the coarse moduli space $\overline{M}_{11,1}$, with the main result stated in Theorem \ref{P11 is open subset of coarse noduli M11 after deleting codim 2 subsets}. In Section \ref{Section: result on chow gp}, we focus on the proof of Theorem \ref{CH2 is tautologically generated for rationally connected moduli space introduction}. In Section \ref{Section: Last section}, we combine these results to conclude the proof of Theorem \ref{My work}.\\
\\
\indent \textbf{Acknowledgments} The author is deeply grateful to his advisor, Qizheng Yin, for suggesting the topic of this project and for his invaluable guidance and insight throughout its completion. His encouragement was essential to this work.\\
\indent The author also thanks Samir Canning, Chunyi Li, Zhiyuan Li, Zhiyu Tian and Liang Xiao for useful conversations. The author is especially grateful to Yuchen Liu for a very helpful discussion, which led directly to the proof of Theorem \ref{CH2 is tautologically generated for rationally connected moduli space introduction}.\\
\indent This work was partially carried out during the author's visit to the University of Chicago during the REU program. The author thanks Peter May for his hospitality and for organizing the program.\\
\indent The author is also indebted to his parents and family for their unwavering support throughout his studies.
sketch: The proof of Theorem~\ref{My work} uses Mukai's program for genus $11$: the birational map $\phi:\mathcal P\dashrightarrow \cM_{11}$ (Theorem~\ref{Mukai's program}) gives a “birational bridge between the moduli space of K3 surfaces and the moduli space of curves,” so that one can “transfer the problem to a problem about the moduli space of curves.” Concretely, the argument reduces to showing that $\operatorname{CH}^2(\cS_{11}')_\mathbb{Q}$ “can be controlled by” $\operatorname{CH}^2(\cF_{11}')_\mathbb{Q}$ together with $\operatorname{CH}^2(\overline{M}_{11,1})_\mathbb{Q}$. A second ingredient is Theorem~\ref{CH2 is tautologically generated for rationally connected moduli space introduction}: if $\overline{M}_{g,n}$ is rationally connected, then $\operatorname{CH}^2(\overline{M}_{g,n})_\mathbb{Q}$ is generated by tautological classes. Using \cite[Corollary 2]{Bar} that $\overline{M}_{11,1}$ is rationally connected, one gets that $\operatorname{CH}^2(\overline{M}_{11,1})_\mathbb{Q}$ is tautologically generated; this “complete description,” combined with Mukai’s bridge, “allows us to conclude the proof of Theorem~\ref{My work}.”

mcq.question: Let $g=11$ and consider the morphism $\pi:\cS_{g}'\to \cF_{g}'$. For each closed point $x\in \cF_{g}'$, set $S_x:=\pi^{-1}(x)$. For every class $a\in \CH^2(\cS_{g}')$, which statement holds for every such closed point $x$ and class $a$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For every closed point $x\in \cF_{11}'$ and every class $a\in \CH^2(\cS_{11}')$, the restriction $a|_{S_x}$ is a multiple of the Beauville--Voisin class $o_{S_x}$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For every closed point $x\in \cF_{11}'$ and every class $a\in \CH^2(\cS_{11}')_\Q$, the restriction $a|_{S_x}$ lies in the \emph{tautological} subring of $\CH^2(S_x)_\Q$, hence in particular is a multiple of the Beauville--Voisin class $o_{S_x}$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every closed point $x\in \cF_{11}'$ and every class $a\in \CH^2(\cS_{11}')_\Q$, the restriction $a|_{S_x}$ is a multiple of the Beauville--Voisin class $o_{S_x}$ in $\CH^2(S_x)_\Q$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists a dense open subset $U\subset \cF_{11}'$ such that for every closed point $x\in U$ and every class $a\in \CH^2(\cS_{11}')$, the restriction $a|_{S_x}$ is a multiple of the Beauville--Voisin class $o_{S_x}$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For every closed point $x\in \cF_{11}'$ and every class $a\in \CH^2(\cS_{11}')$, the restriction $a|_{S_x}$ is a multiple of the Beauville--Voisin class $o_{S_x}$, and moreover the multiple depends only on the class $\pi_*a\in \CH^2(\cF_{11}')$.

mcq.question:
Let $g\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ have Fourier transform satisfying the decay condition $|\hat g(\xi)|\le C e^{-a|\xi|^m}$ for some constants $m>1$, $C>0$, and $a\in(1,\infty)$. Let $\tau_1,\tau_2\in\mathbb{R}^+$ satisfy
\[
\tau_1<\left(\frac{2}{(2\pi)^{m/(m-1)}(ma)^{-1/(m-1)}e}\right)^{\frac{m-1}{m}},\qquad \tau_2<\left(\frac{2}{ame}\right)^{\frac{1}{m}}.
\]
Define
\[
\Lambda=\{(\pm\tau_1 n^{\frac{m-1}{m}},\,\pm\tau_2 n^{\frac{1}{m}}):\ n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
\]
For arbitrary $f,h\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$, which statement is true for every such pair $(f,h)$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For all $f,h\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$, one has $|V_g(f)(\lambda)|=|V_g(h)(\lambda)|$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ if and only if $f=e^{i\alpha}h$ for some $\alpha\in[0,2\pi)$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For all $f,h\in L^2(\mathbb R)$, one has $|V_g(f)(\lambda)|=|V_g(h)(\lambda)|$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ if and only if $f=e^{i\alpha}h$ for some $\alpha\in[0,2\pi)$, provided the bounds on $\tau_1,\tau_2$ are allowed with $\le$ (i.e. $\tau_1\le\left(\frac{2}{(2\pi)^{m/(m-1)}(ma)^{-1/(m-1)}e}\right)^{\frac{m-1}{m}}$ and $\tau_2\le\left(\frac{2}{ame}\right)^{\frac{1}{m}}$).

choices.label: C
choices.text: If $f=e^{i\alpha}h$ for some $\alpha\in[0,2\pi)$, then $|V_g(f)(\lambda)|=|V_g(h)(\lambda)|$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For all $f,h\in L^2(\mathbb R)$, if $|V_g(f)(\lambda)|=|V_g(h)(\lambda)|$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, then there exists a measurable phase function $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that $f(t)=e^{i\varphi(t)}h(t)$ for almost every $t\in\mathbb R$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For all $f,h\in L^2(\mathbb R)$, one has $|V_g(f)(\lambda)|=|V_g(h)(\lambda)|$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ if and only if $f=h$ almost everywhere.

post_theorem_intro_text:
In each case, we will see that $\operatorname{AutP}(X)$ can in fact be realized by a finite subgroup of the automorphism group for which $\wg_X$ is nontrivial (see \S \ref{proof:classresult}). 

\begin{remark}  \label{autp:2.2exception}\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
     \normalfont\item[(i)] The result of the theorem is not true for $X$ in family \textnumero 2.2. In this case, the Kleiman-Mori cone $\neo(X)$ is generated by two extremal rays of different types, $C_1$ and $D_1$. Any automorphism of $X$ must keep each invariant, thus acts trivially on $\operatorname{Pic}(X)$. So, $\operatorname{AutP}(X)=0$, but $\wg_X=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
     \item[(ii)] If $X$ is a smooth member of \textnumero 3.9 or \textnumero 4.2, we have an upper bound on $\operatorname{AutP}(X)$ by Proposition \ref{imagealphainweylgroup}. It is not yet known whether the bound is attained in these two cases.
    \item[(iii)] A smooth Fano threefold in families \textnumero 6.1, \dots , \textnumero 10.1 is isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^1 \times S$, where $S$ is a del Pezzo surface of degree at most $5$. For all these cases, Matsuki's Weyl group coincides with the classical Weyl group of root system for the underlying $S$. It is known that the group $\operatorname{AutP}(X)$ is usually much smaller than their complete Weyl group (see \S \ref{autP:P1timesdP}). 
 \end{enumerate}
 \end{remark}

As a consequence, we can compute the first cohomology group of Picard group. We have the following result (see \S \ref{sec:H1}).
\begin{thm}  \label{thm:H1main}
    Let $X$ be a smooth Fano threefold with Picard rank $\rho \leq 5$. Let $G\subseteq \operatorname{Aut}(X)$ be a finite group. Then $H^1(G,\operatorname{Pic}(X))=0$.
\end{thm}
In fact, the group $H^1(G,\operatorname{Pic}(X))$ is known even for $\rho \geq 6$ since the first cohomology groups of del Pezzo surfaces are known. 

\subsection*{Outline} We begin with some preliminaries in \S \ref{sec:preliminaries}. In \S\ref{imalphasection}, we recall the Weyl group of a smooth Fano threefold as defined by K. Matsuki. We also show that the group $\operatorname{AutP}(X)$ is bounded above by this Weyl group. Consequently, we obtain that $\operatorname{AutP}(X)$ is trivial for a majority of the families of smooth Fano threefolds. Section \ref{proof:classresult} is divided into ten subsections, each of which discusses the classification of $\operatorname{AutP}(X)$ for a class of families for which $\wg_X$ is nontrivial. In this way, we complete the proof of Theorem \ref{them:classresult}. In \S \ref{sec:H1}, we discuss the first cohomology group of Picard group of smooth Fano threefolds and provide a proof of Theorem \ref{thm:H1main}. Finally, a table summarizing the entire classification is given in \S \ref{table}. 

\subsection*{Acknowledgements} I am grateful to my advisor, Alexander Duncan, for suggesting the problem and for his guidance. 
I also wish to thank Kenji Matsuki for helpful correspondence regarding family \textnumero~3.13.

mcq.question: Let $r,s,t$ be nonzero integers. Which statement is universally true for every such choice of $r,s,t$?

correct_choice.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number $\frac{r+t}{rst}$ is the limit of a non-constant sequence of \emph{non-free} rational numbers \emph{all lying in} $[-4,4]$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number $\frac{r+t}{rst}$ is a limit of a sequence of non-free rational numbers (not necessarily non-constant).

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists a single non-constant sequence $(q_n)\subset\mathbb{Q}$ of non-free rational numbers, depending only on $r,s,t$, such that for every choice of parameters $(a_1,\dots,a_5)\in\mathbb{Z}^5$ the numbers $q_n$ satisfy the corresponding half-relations from \cite{Smilga2021} and $\lim_{n\to\infty} q_n=\frac{r+t}{rst}$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The number $\frac{r+t}{rst}$ is the limit of a non-constant sequence of \emph{integer} non-free rational numbers.

post_theorem_intro_text:
We obtain these values by explicitly constructing simplicial $2$-complexes that have this diameter. It is worth noting that the previously best known lower bound \cite{bohman2022complexes},  with error term of order $d^2/(\log d)^\varepsilon$, was obtained by random methods.

One way to obtain a simplicial $2$-complex with large diameter, formulated in graph theoretic language, is to build a long \emph{trail-square}, that is, a sequence of (not necessarily distinct) vertices such that every pair of vertices occurs at most once within distance two in the sequence.
For example, any ordering of the vertex set provides such a sequence, and the pairs appearing at distance at most two in the sequence form the square\towriteornottowrite{\footnote{The \emph{square} $G^{(2)}$ of a graph $G$ is the graph defined on the vertex set $V(G)$ by connecting the pairs of vertices whose distance in $G$ is at most two.}}{} of a Hamilton path.
But this is only a linear number of pairs however, while in an optimal trail-square we are aiming to cover (almost) all the pairs. 
Our initial approach to this problem was to create a large family of pairwise edge-disjoint squares of Hamilton paths and ``glue’’ them up into a trail-square with the introduction of a new vertex or two at each connection.
How much these new vertices can be reused at more than one connection might depend on the ends of the squares of Hamilton paths being ``well-distributed''.
To gain flexibility in that regard, a decomposition of the edges of the complete graph into squares of Hamilton cycles proves to be quite handy, since each can then be ``cut’’ anywhere to obtain a family of pairwise edge-disjoint squares of Hamilton paths with a good variety of endings.
This leads us to the following natural\towriteornottowrite{, purely graph-theoretical }{ }question:

\begin{question}
\label{quest:HC2}
For which positive integers $n$ can the edge set of $K_n$ be partitioned into squares of Hamilton cycles?
\end{question}

\towriteornottowrite{Unless $n=3$ or $4$, the square of a Hamilton cycle is 4-regular. Consequently for $n\geq 5$, a partition of $E(K_n)$ into squares of Hamilton cycles can only exist if each vertex degree is divisible by 4, i.e.\@ $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.}{
 In case a partition of $E(K_n)$ into squares of Hamilton cycles exists, one certainly needs that each vertex has a degree that is divisible by $4$. Hence $n$ being congruent to $1 \pmod 4$ is a necessary condition.}
 This is also conjectured to be sufficient, at least for large enough $n$, as a special case of a general conjecture about packing bounded degree graphs into the complete graph~\cite[Conjecture~1.4]{Oberwolfach}.

The answer to the analogous question about Hamilton cycles has been known since at least 1892.
A construction, which exists for all odd $n$, is attributed to Walecki (see \cite{Walecki} and \cite{alspach2008wonderful}).
The work of Ferber, Lee, and Mousset~\cite{FerberLeeMousset} proves the existence of families of pairwise edge-disjoint squares of Hamilton cycles which cover all but $o(n^2)$ edges of $K_n$.

Here we exhibit an explicit construction of a perfect decomposition of the edges of the complete graph into squares of Hamilton cycles for an infinite sequence of $n$. 

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:packHC2}
    Let $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ be a prime number, such that the order $\ord_p(2)$ of $2$ modulo $p$ is divisible by four. Then $E(K_p)$ can be partitioned into pairwise edge-disjoint copies of $C_p^2$. This is the case in particular if $p\equiv 5 \pmod 8$.
\end{theorem}

For our application, this theorem is more advantageous to use than the unspecified $o(n^2)$ error term of~\cite{FerberLeeMousset}. This is because for any $n$ there is a prime $p \in [n-n^{0.53},n]$ which satisfies $p \equiv 5 \pmod 8$,~\cite{Kumchev_consecutive_arithmetic}, so we can cover all but $\mathcal O(n^{1.53})$ edges of $K_n$ by squares of long cycles. Cutting these appropriately and connecting them up into a long trail-square with the introduction of a couple of new vertices in between, one can make sure that only $n^{1.53}$ edges of $K_n$ are not being covered. This way we end up with a construction of diameter $\frac{1}{2} \binom{n}{2} - \mathcal O(n^{1.53})$, already improving the result from~\cite{bohman2022complexes} for $d=2$. 

In relation to Theorem~\ref{thm:main, 4k+1}, for $n=p$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:packHC2} one can make the gluing described above a bit more efficient, so it leaves out only a linear number of edges. 
It turns out however that this can not be improved in general if we insist on a trail-square construction. 
Indeed, if a simplicial $2$-complex is constructed in the trail-square manner, then for any $i\in [n]$ which is not among the first or last two elements of the sequence, the number of $2$-sets of the simplicial complex containing $i$ is a multiple of four. 
Thus, when restricted to vertex-sequential, there is an infinite sequence of $n$, those where $n-1$ is not divisible by four, where the error term will be of order $\Omega (n)$.

Since in Theorem \ref{thm:main, 4k+1}, we want to match the upper bound for all $n$, we have to do it differently and consider simplicial complexes that are not of the vertex-sequential form.
This will be introduced in Section~\ref{sec:Thm1.1}. 
The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:packHC2} is given in Sections~\ref{sec:proofHC2}.
In the concluding remarks, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}, we mention a generalization of the ``partition/cut/glue'' approach to $d \ge 3$ and contemplate about a couple of open problems/conjectures, in particular, continue the discussion of Question~\ref{quest:HC2}.
sketch:
We obtain the values in Theorem~\ref{thm:main, 4k+1} by “explicitly constructing simplicial $2$-complexes that have this diameter.” The initial proof strategy is described in graph-theoretic terms: build a long “trail-square,” i.e. “a sequence of (not necessarily distinct) vertices such that every pair of vertices occurs at most once within distance two in the sequence,” aiming to “cover (almost) all the pairs.” The proposed method is to “create a large family of pairwise edge-disjoint squares of Hamilton paths and ‘glue’ them up into a trail-square with the introduction of a new vertex or two at each connection,” and to gain flexibility by using “a decomposition of the edges of the complete graph into squares of Hamilton cycles,” which can be “cut” to get many edge-disjoint squares of Hamilton paths.

An explicit decomposition result (Theorem~\ref{thm:packHC2}) is then used for the construction: using primes $p\equiv 5\pmod 8$ near $n$, “we can cover all but $\mathcal O(n^{1.53})$ edges of $K_n$ by squares of long cycles. Cutting these appropriately and connecting them up into a long trail-square with the introduction of a couple of new vertices in between,” one ensures “only $n^{1.53}$ edges of $K_n$ are not being covered,” yielding “a construction of diameter $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{2}-\mathcal O(n^{1.53})$.” For $n=p$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:packHC2}, “one can make the gluing described above a bit more efficient, so it leaves out only a linear number of edges.”

post_theorem_intro_text:
\medskip
Our approach combines three key ingredients: (i) a local energy inequality for biharmonic functions, (ii) a hole-filling iteration lemma with singular factors, and (iii) a mean value inequality applied to the Laplacian of $u$. A central step is an $L^2$-estimate for $\Delta u$, which may be viewed as the biharmonic analogue of the classical Caccioppoli inequality
(see \eqref{ineq:Cacciopoli_laplacian}). This estimate is reminiscent of Maz’ya–Mayboroda’s work in the Euclidean case, but adapted here to the setting of manifolds with Ricci curvature bounded below. Once this estimate is in place, we show that subquadratic growth forces $\Delta u \equiv 0$, thereby reducing the problem to Yau’s theorem. We must observe that the proof of our Caccioppoli-type inequality \eqref{ineq:Cacciopoli_laplacian} is somewhat delicate, as the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Caccio-1-biharmonic-Br} depends on a cut-off dependent
application of Young's inequality.

\medskip
In some sense Theorem \ref{thm:main} is sharp: in $\mathbb{R}^n$ any biharmonic function of subquadratic growth is in fact harmonic of linear growth, showing that the quadratic threshold cannot be weakened. Our theorem thus provides a natural extension of Liouville property to biharmonic functions in manifolds of nonnegative Ricci curvature, which is a natural higher-order extension of Yau’s Liouville theorem, and a foundational step toward $k$-polyharmonic analogues.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Organization of the paper.} The material in this paper is presented as follows. In Section \ref{section:technical} we collect some technical facts (which can be safely said that are 
 standard tools by now), in Section \ref{sect:Cacciopoli} we introduce
 some local energy estimates and Caccioppoli-type inequalities for
 biharmonic functions, and in Section \ref{sect:proof_main_thm} we prove our main result.
sketch: Our approach combines three key ingredients: (i) a local energy inequality for biharmonic functions, (ii) a hole-filling iteration lemma with singular factors, and (iii) a mean value inequality applied to the Laplacian of $u$. A central step is an $L^2$-estimate for $\Delta u$, viewed as the biharmonic analogue of the classical Caccioppoli inequality (see \eqref{ineq:Cacciopoli_laplacian}), adapted to manifolds with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge 0$. Once this estimate is in place, we show that subquadratic growth forces $\Delta u \equiv 0$, thereby reducing the problem to Yau’s theorem. The proof of the Caccioppoli-type inequality \eqref{ineq:Cacciopoli_laplacian} is somewhat delicate, since Lemma \ref{lem:Caccio-1-biharmonic-Br} depends on a cut-off dependent application of Young's inequality.

mcq.question: Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature $\mathrm{Ric}\ge 0$. Let $u\in C^4(M)$ be a biharmonic function (i.e. $\Delta^2 u=0$) of subquadratic growth (for example, with $r(x)=\mathrm{dist}(x,x_0)$, $|u(x)|=o(r(x)^2)$ as $r(x)\to\infty$). Which statement is true for every such $u$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: Every such biharmonic function $u$ must be harmonic (i.e. $\Delta u=0$); in particular, any biharmonic function on $M$ of sublinear growth (e.g. $|u(x)|=o(r(x))$) must be constant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every such biharmonic function $u$ must be harmonic (i.e. $\Delta u=0$) provided $u$ has at most quadratic growth, e.g. $|u(x)|=O(r(x)^2)$ as $r(x)\to\infty$; in particular, any biharmonic function of at most linear growth must be constant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every such biharmonic function $u$ must satisfy that $\Delta u$ is a constant function on $M$ (equivalently, $u$ is harmonic up to an additive quadratic polynomial term).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every such biharmonic function $u$ must be constant; in particular, any biharmonic function on $M$ of subquadratic growth is identically constant.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every such biharmonic function $u$ must be harmonic (i.e. $\Delta u=0$) assuming only that $\mathrm{Ric}\ge -K$ for some constant $K\ge 0$ (with the same subquadratic growth hypothesis); in particular, any biharmonic function of sublinear growth must be constant.

sketch_usage_meta.label: C

sketch_usage_meta.label: D

sketch_usage_meta.label: E

The options differ in subtle but essential ways (subquadratic vs quadratic, harmonic vs constant, Ric ≥ 0 vs Ric ≥ −K).

theorem.content:
\label{Proposition:Phi:compact}
    The input-output operator $\Psi:L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact.
theorem.label: Proposition:Phi:compact

sketch: Let $(f_k)_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a bounded sequence in $L^2(\Omega\times (0,T))$. By Proposition \ref{proposition:existence:strong:solutions}, the associated weak solutions $(y(\cdot,,\cdot,f_k))_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ are bounded in $C^0([0,T];H_0^1(\Omega))$. Hence the terminal states $Y_k:=y(\cdot,T,f_k)$ form a bounded sequence in $H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$. Using the compact Sobolev-Gagliardo-Nirenberg embedding $H_0^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)$, there exists a subsequence of $(Y_k)$ converging strongly in $L^2(\Omega)$. Therefore $\Psi$ maps bounded sets into relatively compact sets in $L^2(\Omega)$, i.e. $\Psi$ is compact, proving Proposition~\ref{Proposition:Phi:compact}.
expanded_theorem:
\label{Proposition:Phi:compact}
    The input-output operator $\Psi:L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact.

mcq.question: Let $T>0$ and let $\Psi: L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ denote the input-output operator. Which statement is true about $\Psi$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: The operator $\Psi: L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The operator $\Psi: L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact provided that $\Omega$ is bounded (no regularity assumption on $\partial\Omega$) and $\alpha,\beta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\alpha(x)\ge \alpha_0>0$ a.e. in $\Omega$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The operator $\Psi: L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is bounded (continuous).

choices.label: D
choices.text:
There exists a constant $C>0$ depending only on $\alpha_0$, $\|\alpha\|_{W^{1,\infty}}$, $\||\vec{\sigma}|\|_{L^\infty}$, $\|p\|_\infty$, $\Omega$ and $T$ such that for every $h\in L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))$ one has the estimate
\[
\|\Psi(h)\|_{H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\|h\|_{L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))},
\]
and in particular $\Psi: L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The operator $\Psi: L^2(0,T;L^2(\Omega))\to L^2(\Omega)$ is compact only if the Sobolev embedding $H_0^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)$ is continuous but not necessarily compact (so compactness of $\Psi$ does not rely on any compact embedding).

sketch_usage_meta.label: C
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: drop compactness conclusion; keep mere continuity of the input-output map

sketch_usage_meta.label: D
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: upgrading output to $H_0^1\cap H^2$ with uniform estimate for all $h$ (overstates terminal-time regularity/estimate)

ALS.justification: The stem does not state or strongly hint that compactness is the correct property; several options mention compactness under differing conditions, so the correct choice is not leaked directly.

TAS.justification: As written, it largely functions as a recall/check-the-box item about a single asserted property of an operator (“is Ψ compact?”). If the surrounding material contained a theorem stating compactness of Ψ, then choice A is close to a direct restatement.

GPS.justification: Some reasoning is invited (compactness vs mere boundedness; role of regularity/embeddings), but the operator Ψ is not defined beyond being an “input-output operator,” so the student cannot genuinely derive compactness from first principles—this makes the item more about recognizing the intended theorem than generating an argument.

DQS.justification: Distractors are thematically aligned (boundedness-only, overstrong regularity estimate, conditional compactness, misunderstanding of compact embeddings). However, several are wordy/technical and the plausibility depends heavily on missing assumptions about Ψ (PDE, boundary regularity, smoothing), making the distractor set feel more like ‘theorem-fragment matching’ than well-posed alternatives.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: Moderate-quality MCQ: it avoids explicit answer leakage and includes reasonably targeted distractors, but it is under-specified (Ψ is not defined), making the truth of compactness ambiguous. In typical context it likely reduces to recalling a stated result rather than testing genuinely generative reasoning.

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main}
    The properad $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}_{prop}$ is Koszul contractible, and therefore it is a Koszul properad.
theorem.label: thm:main

sketch:
To establish Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, the text says one combines two ingredients: (1) it was proven in \cite{emprin2025properadic} that the dioperad $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}$ is contractible; and (2) one uses “a geometric interpretation of the bar complexes associated to (the Koszul dual of) the planar dioperad $\scrY^{(n)}_{pl}$”, via moduli spaces of (polynomial) quadratic differentials on $\CC$ with a “non-compact cell complex structure”.

In the $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}$ case specifically, “one needs to remove a certain subcomplex of \emph{cloven Strebel differentials}.” The argument then uses “geometric arguments” to “control the topology of this subcomplex,” concluding it is “always homologous to a bouquet of $(k-2)$-spheres, where $k$ is the number of outputs.” Finally, “together with a comparison between the bar complexes associated to $\mathscr{V}^{(n)}$ and $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}$, vanishing of this homology outside of that specific degree implies vanishing of higher cohomology of the relevant bar complex, establishing our main theorem.”

To prove the main theorem, the text says one combines two ingredients: (1) it was proven in emprin2025properadic that the dioperad $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}$ is contractible; and (2) one uses “a geometric interpretation of the bar complexes associated to (the Koszul dual of) the planar dioperad $\scrY^{(n)}_{pl}$”, via moduli spaces of (polynomial) quadratic differentials on $\CC$ with a “non-compact cell complex structure”.

In the $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}$ case specifically, “one needs to remove a certain subcomplex of \emph{cloven Strebel differentials}.” The argument then uses “geometric arguments” to “control the topology of this subcomplex,” concluding it is “always homologous to a bouquet of $(k-2)$-spheres, where $k$ is the number of outputs.” Finally, “together with a comparison between the bar complexes associated to $\mathscr{V}^{(n)}$ and $\mathscr{Y}^{(n)}$, vanishing of this homology outside of that specific degree implies vanishing of higher cohomology of the relevant bar complex, establishing the main theorem.”

theorem.content:
\label{theorem:main}
Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb R^n$ be an open set and 
$(X, d, z_0)$ be a pointed complete metric space.
Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be a Lipschitz continuous mapping. Then
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item there exists a map from $\Omega$ to the space of bounded linear operators 
$\nabla^{\circ}f:\Omega \to \mathcal L(\mathbb R^n; \left(\textnormal{Lip}_{z_0}(X)\right)^*)$
such that for $\varphi\in \textnormal{Lip}_{z_0}(X)$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$
\begin{equation}
\langle \varphi, \nabla^{\circ}f(x)\cdot\nu \rangle = \nabla\varphi\circ f(x)\cdot\nu \label{eq:nabla0}
\end{equation}
whenever $\varphi\circ f$ is classically differentiable; and
\item there exists a seminorm $\rho$ on $\left(\textnormal{Lip}_{z_0}(X)\right)^*$
such that for $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$
\[
\textnormal{md}(f, x)(\nu) = \rho(\nabla^{\circ}f(x)\cdot\nu)
\]
for almost every $x\in\Omega$.
\end{enumerate}

post_theorem_intro_text:
Naturally, our notion of differential relates to other linearized interpretations of metric differential,
for example, the one introduced by Gigli, Pasqualetto, and Soultanis in \cite{GPS2020}.
The primary difference lies in the target spaces of the differentials. 
However, both constructions coincide when representing the metric differential of a Lipschitz mapping
(see \cite[Theorem 4.7]{GPS2020} and Lemma \ref{lemma:md=rho}).

In (ii) of Theorem \ref{theorem:main}, $\rho$ appears as a seminorm, which accounts for the possible non-separability of the target space. When the target is separable, it is, in fact, a norm.
Our primary tool is the notion of weak weak* derivatives, which are essentially characterized by condition \eqref{eq:nabla0}. 
Such partial derivatives were introduced in \cite{CE:23} and \cite{CE:2021} and naturally arise for mappings that are absolutely continuous on almost every line, especially when the target space is not a dual of a separable Banach space or lacks the Radon–Nikodým property.
In this paper, we occasionally develop further properties of these derivatives. In particular, it is shown the measurability of the norm and 
\[
\|\partial_j^{\circ} f(x)\|_ {\left(\textnormal{Lip}_{z_0}(X)\right)^*} = 
\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{d(f(x+h\cdot e_j),f(x))}{|h|} \quad \text{ for almost every }  x\in\Omega
\]
Whenever $f$ has a locally integrable partial metric derivative.

\subsection{Organization.}
The paper is organized as follows.
In Section \ref{sec1} we collect necessary results
and definitions concerning the calculus of functions with values in metric spaces.
Then in Section \ref{sec2} we discuss the core object -- weak weak* derivatives. Essentially, in this section, we prove part (i) of  Theorem \ref{theorem:main}.
Section \ref{sec4} is devoted to the metric differentiability and part (ii) ot Theorem \ref{theorem:main} is proved there.
As well, we discuss metric differentiability in the topology of the Sobolev norm.
Finally, in Section \ref{sec5} we consider the case of a linear target.

Let $g,K$ and $M$ be integers such that $g\geq 3$, $K$ is sufficiently large in terms of $g$, and $M\in (g^{K-1},g^{K}]$. Suppose that $k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}$ fulfil \cref{k cond S} and \cref{k cond N}, then

\[r_{S_1+S_2+S_3}(M)\]

They then pass from representations by $S_i$ to representations by the Niven subsets $\mathcal N_i=\{n\in S_g(k_i):\ k_i\mid n\}$: \emph{“By showing that a proportion of such representations have each summand being a Niven number, we provide a lower bound for the number of representations of $M$ as the sum of three Niven numbers.”} This is made precise by imposing additional coprimality conditions $(k_i,k_j)=1$ and $(k_i,g)=1$ and relating
\[r_{\mathcal N_1+\mathcal N_2+\mathcal N_3}(M)\]
to $r_{S_1+S_2+S_3}(M)$ with an explicit main factor plus error term (Theorem~\ref{Main theorem N count}). Finally, they note that Theorem~\ref{Main theorem 1} follows \emph{as a corollary} of Theorem~\ref{Main theorem N count} \emph{“after showing that such a choice of $k_1,k_2$ and $k_3$ exist.”}

mcq.question: Let $g$ be any integer with $g\ge 3$. Call a positive integer $n$ a base-$g$ Niven number if $n$ is divisible by the sum of its base-$g$ digits, and let $\mathcal N_g$ be the set of all base-$g$ Niven numbers. Which statement is universally true for every such $g$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For every integer $g\ge 3$, the set $\mathcal N_g$ is an asymptotic basis of order $3$; equivalently, there exists $N_0(g)$ such that every integer $N\ge N_0(g)$ can be written as a sum of three base-$g$ Niven numbers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For every integer $g\ge 3$, the set $\mathcal N_g$ is an asymptotic basis of order $2$; equivalently, there exists $N_0(g)$ such that every integer $N\ge N_0(g)$ can be written as a sum of two base-$g$ Niven numbers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every integer $g\ge 3$, the set $\mathcal N_g$ is an asymptotic basis of some finite order; equivalently, there exist an integer $s=s(g)$ and $N_0(g)$ such that every integer $N\ge N_0(g)$ can be written as a sum of $s$ base-$g$ Niven numbers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For every integer $g\ge 3$, there exists an absolute constant $N_0$ (independent of $g$) such that every integer $N\ge N_0$ can be written as a sum of three base-$g$ Niven numbers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For every integer $g\ge 3$, there exists $N_0(g)$ such that every integer $N\ge N_0(g)$ can be written as a sum of three base-$g$ Niven numbers $n_1+n_2+n_3$ with each $n_i$ having base-$g$ digit sum exactly equal to the mean $\mu_K=(g-1)K/2$ among $K$-digit numbers.

ALS.justification: The stem only defines base-g Niven numbers and asks which statement holds for all g≥3. It does not hint at “order 3” or otherwise single out choice A; the correct option is not telegraphed by wording or definitions.

TAS.justification: This is not a restatement of the definition of Niven numbers; it asks for a genuinely global additive-basis property (order 2 vs 3 vs some finite order vs uniformity in g vs extra digit-sum constraints). The options compete on nontrivial conclusions.

GPS.justification: Selecting the universally true statement requires substantial mathematical judgment about additive bases and distribution of Niven numbers (e.g., why 2 is too small, why 3 suffices, why uniform N0 is too strong, why exact-mean digit-sum is too rigid). The correct choice is not obvious without real reasoning or specific theorem knowledge.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common failure modes: (B) overstrong minimal order claim, (C) weaker-but-true sounding statement, (D) incorrect uniformity/effectivity across g, (E) plausible probabilistic/typical-digit-sum strengthening that is generally false. They are distinct and aligned with realistic confusions.
